prompt.context: Our client is a start-up with the ability to deliver broadband internet to commercial airlines.
prompt.question: How would you help them think about their offering?

clarifying_info.q: How does the pricing model work?
clarifying_info.a: The start-up would charge customers on a per-flight pricing model.

clarifying_info.q: How much does the start-up need to invest up front?
clarifying_info.a: The start-up would have to invest relatively little up front and would keep most of the revenues.

clarifying_info.q: How many planes are in scope?
What revenue threshold is needed for profitability per plane?
clarifying_info.a: If the company can generate $250,000 per plane in annual revenue, they will be profitable installing the technology on that plane.

clarifying_info.q: How many flights does a plane fly per year?
clarifying_info.a: Each plane flies 2,000 legs per year.

exhibits.title: Airline Seat & Passenger Breakdown
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down seats per plane and traveler characteristics by class (First and Coach), including seat counts, load factor, and the share of business travelers
exhibits.data: First class: 20 seats, 0.75 load factor; Coach: 180 seats, 0.75 load factor; Business traveler share: First 100%, Coach 30%

exhibits.title: Price vs. Penetration Rate
exhibits.shows: A table or chart showing user adoption rates at different price points per flight for broadband internet
exhibits.data: 30 users at $5, 25 users at $10, 20 users at $15, 10 users at $20, 5 users at $25 (per 100 passengers)

framework: Industry & Market attractiveness: size of addressable market, growth trends, customer demand for in-flight broadband
Competitive landscape: existing players, IP/patents, low-speed alternatives
Product & offering: pricing model, features, differentiation
Financials: market size, revenue potential, breakeven analysis, upfront investment
Risks & barriers: regulatory, technical, adoption, competitive response
Go-to-market: airline partnerships, customer acquisition, rollout strategy

questions.prompt: Estimate the total annual addressable market in terms of potential user-legs (Exhibit 1 provided).
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate full seats per plane by applying load factor, then identify laptop users (business travelers) and sum across both classes, then multiply by planes and annual legs.

math.setup: First class: 20 seats × 0.75 load = 15 passengers, all business travelers = 15 laptop users. Coach: 180 seats × 0.75 load = 135 passengers, 30% business = 40.5 laptop users. Total laptop users per plane ≈ 55.5 ≈ 50 (rounded). 3,000 planes × 2,000 legs/plane × 50 laptop users/plane.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, determine the optimal price per flight to maximize revenue per flight.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate revenue at each price point (price × users per 100 passengers) and identify the maximum. $15 yields the highest revenue at $300 per 100 passengers per flight.

math.setup: Assume 100 passengers. Calculate revenue = price × number of users at that price for each option.
math.answer: Optimal price is $15/flight, generating $300 per 100 passengers per flight

questions.prompt: Calculate the breakeven number of users per leg, and determine whether the company will be profitable at the recommended price.
questions.guidance: Candidate should convert the annual profitability threshold of $250,000 per plane into a per-leg revenue requirement, then divide by price to get required users per leg, and compare to expected users at $15.

math.setup: Annual revenue needed per plane: $250,000. Legs per plane per year: 2,000. Required revenue per leg: $250,000 / 2,000. At $15 price, required users = required revenue per leg / $15. Compare to expected users at $15 (20% of ~50 laptop users).
steps: Required users per leg at $15: $125 / $15 ≈ 8 users/leg
Expected users per leg: 50 laptop users × 20% penetration at $15 = 10 users/leg
math.answer: Yes, the company should break even. Expected 10 users per leg exceeds the required 8 users per leg to break even.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should the company consider before entering this market?

categories.name: Competition & IP
ideas: The company holds the patent on the high-speed connection — strong competitive moat
Threat from low-speed internet alternatives already on some planes
Future competitors could enter if patent expires or is designed around

categories.name: Risks
ideas: Low adoption if passengers do not perceive value
Technical reliability and connectivity at altitude
Airlines may negotiate down the revenue share
Cybersecurity vulnerabilities on shared in-flight networks
Dependency on airline partners for installation and distribution

categories.name: Market Dynamics
ideas: Airline industry is cyclical; capacity can shrink in downturns
Business traveler segment is most valuable but may use phone hotspots
Growth potential as broadband demand increases globally

categories.name: Operational Considerations
ideas: Installation coordination with each airline partner
Customer service and technical support model
Billing and authentication infrastructure per flight

recommendation: Enter the market — the economics are favorable at $15/flight pricing, which exceeds the breakeven threshold of 8 users per leg with an estimated 10 users per leg
The patent on high-speed connection provides a defensible competitive advantage
The total addressable market of 300 million annual user-legs represents a large revenue opportunity with limited upfront investment required
risks: Low-speed internet substitutes from competitors could erode the addressable market
Adoption rates could be lower than estimated if passengers rely on cellular data
Airline partners may demand a larger revenue share, reducing margins
next_steps: Negotiate partnership agreements with major airlines to begin installation
Conduct a pilot program on a subset of planes to validate adoption and pricing assumptions
Monitor competitive moves around low-speed internet offerings and patent challenges
